Plants spreading by layering; from 5 dm. to 1 m. across, average 5 to 7 dm. high; herbage yellow-green; buds yellow-green turning white on anthesis; flowers average 12 mm. long, upper lip inflexed from 35° - 90° with prominent dorsal ridge usually ending in a shallow notch, galea white to pinkish yellow; lower lip immediately deflexed at juncture with upper lip, petals curling back, central purple stripe in each lobe extending nearly to tip, lateral one on each side of it extending to summit of throat; corolla glabrous within except for minute pubescence on lower lip at throat, a long pubescence of irregular lengths without; glaea ending in 2 lobes 1.5 mm. long, upturned; anthers white, held in curve of upper lip within 1 to 3 mm. of tip; sterile filament 3/5 as long and against lower lip; stigma with fertile stamens.

A logging road follows Sheep Creek into the mountains.  Curtis Creek:  This creek empties into Sheep Creek at  UTM grid reference points 93.1 X 44.6.  The collecting site was on the left hand side of the road while going up the road.
notes: DWJ uses the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) grid for geo location.  Data columns are just after T/R/S columns.  Now, per Google Maps, there is a location called Sheep Creek reached by following Sheep Creek Road.  (Perhaps this was the logging road.)  A short distance (1.2 miles) downstream from the end of Sheep Creek Road, after the New Denver Road fork,  the creek is called Billings Creek  for about .5 miles.  Then Google calls it the Pend Oreille River until it reaches the Salmo River at BC Hwy 3 & 6 and Sheep Creek Road.  Downstream, the Salmo joins the Pend-d'Oreille River, which flows across the border to the US where it's called the Pen Oreille River until it joins the Columbia River.  There is no Curtis Creek in Google Maps.

specimenDescription: Part of a hybrid swarm intermediate between Chamaesyce amplexicaulis, C. punctulata and C. recurva.  Part of the hybrid complex involving EE. amplexicaulis, nummularia, and punctulata that grew at the northwest point of Bartholomew Island.  The plants grew in volcanic ash among lava rocks in a narrow belt less than 100 m. long.  The individuals varied in habit, vestiture, gland-appendages, and seeds, while the leaves varied in size, shape, margin, and color.  Chamaesyce bindloensis may have been one of the elements in the complex.
